newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Mixed as supplies vary.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Mixed as supplies vary.

text.p: The direction on Asia's oil product markets appeared mixed as supplies of different products were varied as the region entered a low-demand period, traders said on Monday.

Gas oil and fuel oil remained under pressure by China's tardy return to the market and ample regional stocks as well as potential supplies coming in from outside the region. But some support was expected from India and Taiwan, traders said.

The gasoline market was largely led by aggressive selling by a trader but the market anticipated supplies to dip amid shutdowns at a number of regional refineries, while naphtha was supported by tight supplies.

The gas oil market was let down by India's purchase of 570,000 tonnes of 1.0-percent sulphur diesel for April deliveries over the weekend, which traders said would have an initial bearish impact on prices. Market consensus last week was that India would take around 700,000 tonnes.
But traders noted that India could still provide some support as it has issued a second tender for April seeking 270,000 tonnes.

China has returned to buy gas oil since early last week, but they have kept their purchase price low and did not appear to be in a rush to buy short term due to ample stocks in the country and in Hong Kong.

Last week, China bought at $202 a tonne for end-February/early March delivery cost-and-freight (c-and-f) southern China, but remained intent on curbing their bids at the $200-mark, while sellers were indicating $204-$205.

Traders also noted that gas oil stocks were kept in check by the continued output cuts of Singapore refineries and the scheduled one-month shutdown at the 280,000-barrel-per-day Mobil Singapore facility from March 15.
Traders said Mobil would soon need to buy more gas oil for its terminal in Hong Kong because of the refinery maintenance.
Regional supplies were kept in check by maintenance shutdowns at another Singapore refinery as well as in Australia and Indonesia.

This was helping gas oil prices to remain steady at around $25.20 per barrel free-on-board (fob) Singapore, despite recent sharp falls in crude and gas oil futures prices on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE).

Traders noted that Asian gas oil prices were about $19 a tonne over that of Europe, while the differential between Mediterranean and Asia was around $25 a tonne. Freight rates have also fallen from their high levels seen late last year.
These factors were making it attractive for several western and Middle East traders to start working on shipping cargoes eastwards.
If these cargoes finally arrive in Asia sometime during end March-early April, it would help to fill the supply gap as a result of the regional shutdowns, traders said.

China has also been "relaxed" in its fuel oil imports as ports were congested. While China had returned to the market, they were reluctant to buy at current levels. China's indications of $107 per tonne c-and-f, were $2-$4 a tonne below seller's indications.

Traders fear that if Chinese demand remained slow, while ample supplies were seen coming from Kuwait, South Korea and Japan, prices in Singapore would again test the $100-mark, fob basis as seen between mid-January and early February.

But some support was seen from Taiwan which was seeking 76,000 tonnes of 0.5-percent sulphur material for early April. India also has additional demand in March for the high sulphur grade, bringing its demand for March to 120,000 tonnes.

Sentiment in the naphtha market was spurred by record high premiums under discussion in term sale talks for more than two million tonnes between Kuwait and Asian buyers for March 1997-February 1998 liftings. The latest indications were at $13-$14 a tonne above MidEast quotes, way over the previous term price of $7.90 for August 1996-September 1997 supplies.
The bullishness came despite slow spot demand from north Asian buyers who have covered their March requirements, traders said.
The gasoline market was already seeing the presence of increased supplies from South Korea as new refining capacity comes onstream.
Korea's LG-Caltex sold North Asia's first gasoline cargo to the US West Coast while Korean refiners have also started to take part in Taiwan's monthly import tenders.
